title: The Second World War in Asia & the Pacific
description: The war in Asia and the Pacific, 1931–1945 — Japanese expansion from Manchuria to Pearl Harbor, occupation and its human cost across Southeast Asia, the Pacific island-hopping campaign, the home fronts, the atomic bombs, and the war's consequences for Asia.

notes.heading: Japanese Expansion: Manchuria and the War in China
notes.body: The Second World War in Asia began years before 1939. Japan, a rapidly modernising empire short of oil, iron and food, came under the control of its military in the 1930s. In **1931** Japanese officers staged an explosion on a railway they owned in **Manchuria** (northeast China), blamed the Chinese, and used it as an excuse to invade; by 1932 they had set up the puppet state of **Manchukuo**. The **League of Nations** condemned the invasion but did nothing effective, and Japan simply left the League — an early sign that aggression would go unpunished. In **1937** full-scale war broke out between Japan and China. Japanese forces advanced along the coast and rivers; in **Nanjing** in late 1937 they killed huge numbers of Chinese civilians and prisoners in an atrocity remembered as the Nanjing Massacre. China, though much weaker industrially, refused to surrender: the Nationalists of **Chiang Kai-shek** and the Communists of **Mao Zedong** formed an uneasy alliance and fought on for eight years, tying down over a million Japanese troops. The war in China cost millions of Chinese lives, most of them civilians.

notes.heading: Pearl Harbor and the Outbreak of the Pacific War
notes.body: Japan's war machine ran on imported oil — and about 80% of it came from the **United States**. As Japan expanded into China and then into French Indochina, the USA, Britain and the Netherlands responded in 1941 with an **oil embargo**. Japan's leaders faced a choice: give up their conquests or seize the oil-rich Dutch East Indies (Indonesia) and risk war with America. They chose war, planning to knock out the US Pacific Fleet with a single blow. On **7 December 1941**, Japanese aircraft launched from six aircraft carriers attacked the American naval base at **Pearl Harbor**, Hawaii, sinking or damaging eight battleships and destroying nearly 200 aircraft; about 2,400 Americans were killed. Crucially, the US aircraft carriers were at sea and survived, and the fuel tanks and repair yards were untouched. The same day, Japan attacked British Malaya, Hong Kong, the Philippines and other targets across the Pacific. The USA declared war on Japan, and Germany declared war on the USA days later — joining the Asian and European wars into one truly global conflict.

notes.heading: Japanese Occupation: POWs and Civilians
notes.body: In six months Japan conquered a vast empire: **Hong Kong** (December 1941), **Malaya and Singapore** (February 1942 — Britain's worst military defeat, with some 80,000 troops surrendering), the **Dutch East Indies**, the **Philippines** and **Burma**. Japan claimed to be freeing Asia from Western empires — 'Asia for the Asians' — but occupation was often brutal. Natural resources were seized for Japan's war effort, local currencies collapsed, and food seizures caused terrible **famines**, such as the Bengal famine of 1943 and the famine in Vietnam in 1944–45, each killing millions. Prisoners of war and Asian labourers were forced to work in appalling conditions — around 60,000 Allied POWs and perhaps 200,000 Asian labourers built the **Burma–Thailand 'Death Railway'**, of whom tens of thousands died of disease, overwork and malnutrition. In China and elsewhere, occupation troops committed widespread atrocities against civilians, and in the occupied Philippines and Korea women were forced into sexual slavery as so-called 'comfort women'. POWs were held in camps where disease and starvation were common; about a quarter of Allied prisoners in Japanese hands did not survive.

notes.heading: The Pacific War: Island Hopping and Key Battles
notes.body: The turning point came just six months after Pearl Harbor. At the **Battle of Midway** (June 1942), American codebreakers discovered Japan's plans, and US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese aircraft carriers — a blow from which Japan's navy never recovered. From then on, the Allies advanced in two drives across the Pacific, using a strategy called '**island hopping**': instead of attacking every Japanese-held island, they captured selected islands as air and naval bases and cut off the rest, leaving them to 'wither on the vine'. Key battles included **Guadalcanal** (1942–43), the first major Allied land victory; the return to the **Philippines** at **Leyte Gulf** (October 1944), the largest naval battle in history; and the savage fights for **Iwo Jima** (February–March 1945) and **Okinawa** (April–June 1945), where Japanese soldiers fought almost to the last man and kamikaze pilots crashed explosive-laden planes into Allied ships. The appalling casualties at Iwo Jima and Okinawa — over 100,000 Japanese and tens of thousands of Allied dead — convinced American leaders that invading Japan itself could cost millions of lives.

notes.heading: The Home Fronts in Asia
notes.body: The war transformed daily life across Asia. In **China**, civilians suffered invasion, bombing and displacement on an enormous scale; tens of millions became refugees, and the Nationalist and Communist forces both mobilised peasants for the long war of resistance. In **Japan**, the war at first brought victories, but from 1943 the home front darkened: rationing tightened, schoolchildren were evacuated to the countryside and put to work in factories, and women replaced men in industry. From late 1944, American **B-29 bombers** based on captured islands rained destruction on Japanese cities; a single firebombing raid on **Tokyo** in March 1945 killed around 100,000 people and left a million homeless. Across occupied **Southeast Asia**, people faced forced labour, food seizures and inflation, but also saw the myth of Western invincibility destroyed — Japan had defeated the British, French and Dutch empires in weeks. In some places, such as Burma and Indonesia, nationalists first collaborated with Japan against the old colonial rulers, then turned against their new occupiers, emerging from the war determined never to be colonised again.

notes.heading: The Atomic Bombs and Japan's Surrender
notes.body: By mid-1945 Japan was defeated but would not surrender: its navy was destroyed, its cities were being burned, and its people were close to starvation, yet its military leaders prepared to fight an invasion. The Allies demanded 'unconditional surrender' at **Potsdam** in July 1945; Japan ignored the ultimatum. The United States had secretly developed the **atomic bomb** through the Manhattan Project, and President Truman decided to use it. On **6 August 1945** the B-29 *Enola Gay* dropped a uranium bomb on **Hiroshima**, destroying the city and killing about 70,000–80,000 people instantly; tens of thousands more died of burns and radiation sickness in the following months. On **8 August** the **Soviet Union** declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria, crushing Japanese forces there. On **9 August** a second atomic bomb destroyed **Nagasaki**, killing around 40,000 instantly. With his council deadlocked, **Emperor Hirohito** personally intervened, and on **15 August 1945** he announced Japan's surrender — the first time most Japanese had ever heard his voice. The formal surrender was signed on 2 September. Historians still debate whether the bombs, the Soviet entry, or both together forced the decision — and whether the bombs were justified.

notes.heading: Consequences: Decolonisation and a Changing China
notes.body: The war reshaped Asia completely. Around **30 million people** died in the Asian and Pacific war, most of them civilians, and China alone lost perhaps 14–20 million. The old European empires never recovered: Britain left **India, Burma and Ceylon** (1947–48), the Dutch fought and lost a war to keep **Indonesia** (independent 1949), and France's attempt to retake **Vietnam** led to decades of conflict. 'Asia for the Asians' had been a Japanese slogan, but the war made it a reality on Asian terms. In **China**, the war had exhausted the Nationalist government, while the Communists emerged stronger and more popular; civil war resumed and in **1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China**, with the Nationalists fleeing to Taiwan — a division that still shapes world politics. **Japan** was occupied by the USA until 1952, given a democratic constitution that renounced war, and rebuilt into an economic superpower. The war's wounds — the treatment of POWs, the 'comfort women', the atomic bombings — remain sensitive issues in Asian politics today, and war-crimes trials in **Tokyo** (1946–48) punished Japanese leaders much as Nuremberg punished the Nazis.

flashcards.definition: The resource-rich region of northeast China invaded by Japan in 1931 after a staged railway explosion; Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo there.
flashcards.example: The League of Nations condemned the invasion but took no action, and Japan simply left the League.

flashcards.definition: The US naval base in Hawaii attacked without warning by Japanese carrier aircraft on 7 December 1941, bringing the USA into the Second World War.
flashcards.example: About 2,400 Americans were killed and eight battleships sunk or damaged, but the US carriers were at sea and survived.

flashcards.definition: The 1941 refusal of the USA, Britain and the Netherlands to sell oil to Japan, which pushed Japan's leaders to choose war rather than abandon their conquests.
flashcards.example: Japan imported about 80% of its oil from the USA, so the embargo threatened to stop its whole war machine.

flashcards.definition: The surrender of some 80,000 British Empire troops to a smaller Japanese force in February 1942 — often called Britain's worst military defeat.
flashcards.example: Singapore's fall shattered the myth that the European empires in Asia could not be beaten.

flashcards.definition: The railway between Burma and Thailand built in 1942–43 by about 60,000 Allied POWs and perhaps 200,000 Asian labourers, tens of thousands of whom died from overwork, disease and malnutrition.
flashcards.example: The railway's human cost made it a lasting symbol of the brutal treatment of prisoners and labourers under Japanese occupation.

flashcards.definition: The June 1942 naval battle in which the USA, forewarned by codebreaking, sank four Japanese aircraft carriers — the turning point of the Pacific War.
flashcards.example: Japan's navy never recovered from losing four carriers and their experienced air crews in a single battle.

flashcards.definition: The Allied Pacific strategy of capturing only selected islands as bases and cutting off the rest, rather than attacking every Japanese-held island.
flashcards.example: Bypassed Japanese garrisons were left isolated and unable to affect the war — 'withering on the vine'.

flashcards.definition: Two savage 1945 battles in which Japanese defenders fought almost to the last man; their huge casualties convinced US leaders that invading Japan could cost millions of lives.
flashcards.example: At Okinawa, kamikaze pilots crashed explosive-laden planes into Allied ships, sinking dozens.

flashcards.definition: Japanese pilots who deliberately crashed explosive-laden aircraft into Allied ships in suicide attacks, mainly in 1944–45.
flashcards.example: Kamikaze attacks caused serious losses in the battles for the Philippines and Okinawa.

flashcards.definition: The two Japanese cities destroyed by American atomic bombs on 6 and 9 August 1945, killing well over 100,000 people and forcing Japan's surrender.
flashcards.example: Hiroshima was hit first by a uranium bomb; Nagasaki was bombed three days later with a plutonium bomb.

flashcards.definition: The emperor of Japan whose personal intervention in August 1945 broke the deadlock in Japan's government and brought surrender; he remained emperor until 1989.
flashcards.example: His radio broadcast of 15 August 1945 was the first time most Japanese had heard their emperor's voice.

flashcards.definition: The process by which Asian colonies won independence from European empires after 1945, accelerated by Japan's defeat of those empires in 1941–42.
flashcards.example: India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon became independent in 1947–48, and Indonesia in 1949.

questions.stem: Which region of China did Japan invade in 1931, setting up the puppet state of Manchukuo?
choices: Tibet
Manchuria
Hong Kong
Mongolia
questions.explanation: Japan invaded Manchuria, the resource-rich northeast of China, in 1931 after staging a railway explosion as an excuse. The League of Nations condemned the invasion but took no effective action.

questions.stem: Why did the failure of the League of Nations over Manchuria matter for the rest of the 1930s?
choices: It proved the League could raise an army
It showed aggressive powers that invasion would go unpunished, encouraging further aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany
It forced Japan to withdraw immediately
It had no effect on anything
questions.explanation: When the League merely condemned Japan and Japan simply walked out, dictators learned a lesson: aggression worked. Mussolini's invasion of Abyssinia and Hitler's expansion in Europe followed the same pattern.

questions.stem: What event on 7 December 1941 brought the United States into the Second World War?
choices: The fall of Singapore
The invasion of Manchuria
The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor
The bombing of Hiroshima
questions.explanation: Japanese carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, killing about 2,400 Americans. The USA declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany declared war on the USA days later.

questions.stem: Why did Japan decide to attack the United States in 1941?
choices: The USA had invaded Japan first
The Allied oil embargo threatened to stop Japan's war machine, and Japan chose to seize the oil-rich Dutch East Indies and knock out the US fleet first
Japan wanted to sell oil to America
Japan attacked by mistake
questions.explanation: Japan imported about 80% of its oil from the USA, so the 1941 embargo forced a choice: abandon the conquests or grab the oil fields of Southeast Asia. Attacking Pearl Harbor was meant to buy time by crippling the US Pacific Fleet.

questions.stem: Why did the attack on Pearl Harbor fail to achieve Japan's long-term goal?
choices: No ships were damaged
The crucial US aircraft carriers were at sea, the base's fuel and repair facilities survived, and the attack united the USA in determination to fight
Japan captured Hawaii and held it until 1945
The USA immediately surrendered
questions.explanation: Japan knocked out battleships but missed the carriers — the decisive weapon of the Pacific War — and left the fuel tanks and repair yards intact. Far from forcing America to negotiate, the attack enraged it into total war.

questions.stem: Why is the fall of Singapore in February 1942 considered such a disaster for Britain?
choices: Singapore was Britain's capital city
Around 80,000 British Empire troops surrendered to a smaller Japanese force, destroying the myth of Western invincibility in Asia
Britain lost no soldiers at Singapore
Singapore was returned to Britain the following week
questions.explanation: The supposedly impregnable fortress of Singapore fell in a week of land fighting, with about 80,000 troops surrendering. Asians had watched a European empire collapse in weeks — a blow to British prestige that helped fuel decolonisation.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes life for prisoners of war and forced labourers under Japanese occupation?
choices: They were treated as honoured guests
They were immediately released
They built projects such as the Burma–Thailand railway in appalling conditions, and tens of thousands died of overwork, disease and starvation
They were given extra food and pay
questions.explanation: Around 60,000 Allied POWs and perhaps 200,000 Asian labourers built the 'Death Railway'; tens of thousands died. About a quarter of Allied prisoners held by Japan did not survive the camps.

questions.stem: Why was the Battle of Midway (June 1942) the turning point of the Pacific War?
choices: It was the first battle fought on Japanese soil
US forces, warned by codebreakers, sank four Japanese aircraft carriers — a loss of ships and air crews from which Japan's navy never recovered
Japan captured Midway and used it to bomb Hawaii
It ended the war immediately
questions.explanation: American codebreaking revealed Japan's plan, and US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers in a single day. Japan could not replace the ships or their veteran pilots, and from Midway onwards it was forced onto the defensive.

questions.stem: What was the Allied strategy of 'island hopping' in the Pacific?
choices: Attacking every Japanese-held island in turn
Capturing only selected islands as air and naval bases while cutting off and bypassing the rest
Retreating from island to island
Sending soldiers on holiday tours of the Pacific
questions.explanation: Island hopping saved time and lives: the Allies seized key islands to use as bases, while bypassed Japanese garrisons were cut off from supply and left unable to affect the war.

questions.stem: How did the battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa influence the decision to use the atomic bomb?
choices: They showed Japanese resistance collapsing, making invasion easy
Their appalling casualties — defenders fighting almost to the last man and kamikaze attacks — convinced US leaders that invading Japan itself could cost millions of lives
They had no influence on any decisions
They led the USA to withdraw from the war
questions.explanation: At Iwo Jima and Okinawa, over 100,000 Japanese soldiers and tens of thousands of Allies died, and civilians suffered terribly. Projecting such resistance onto the Japanese home islands made the atomic bomb look to US leaders like the cheaper option in lives.

questions.stem: How did the war affect ordinary civilians on the home fronts in Asia?
choices: Civilians were completely unaffected
Millions suffered bombing, rationing, forced labour, food seizures and famine; tens of millions of Chinese became refugees
Only soldiers were involved in the war
Food became more plentiful everywhere
questions.explanation: The Asian war was a total war for civilians: China saw tens of millions of refugees, Japan's cities were firebombed, and food seizures caused famines in Bengal and Vietnam that each killed millions.

questions.stem: On which dates and cities were the two atomic bombs dropped in August 1945?
choices: Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August
Tokyo on 6 August and Osaka on 9 August
Nagasaki on 6 August and Hiroshima on 9 August
Both bombs fell on Tokyo on 6 August
questions.explanation: Hiroshima was destroyed by a uranium bomb on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki by a plutonium bomb on 9 August. Between them the bombs killed well over 100,000 people, many dying later from burns and radiation sickness.

questions.stem: What finally broke the deadlock in Japan's government and led to surrender in August 1945?
choices: A vote in the Japanese parliament
Emperor Hirohito's personal intervention after the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war
The resignation of the US president
A peace treaty negotiated with China
questions.explanation: Even after two atomic bombs and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, Japan's leaders were split. Emperor Hirohito broke the deadlock himself, announcing the surrender by radio on 15 August 1945.

questions.stem: Historians debate why Japan surrendered. Which combination of events do most consider decisive?
choices: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki together with the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan
The fall of Singapore
The invention of radar
The arrival of the monsoon season
questions.explanation: Within four days Japan was hit by two atomic bombs and a devastating Soviet invasion of Manchuria, destroying any hope of negotiating through Moscow. Historians argue over which mattered more, but agree the combination forced surrender.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the war's most important consequence for Asia was the end of European empires. Which evidence best supports this view?
choices: Japan's defeat of the Western powers in 1941–42 destroyed their prestige, and within a decade India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon and Indonesia had won independence
The European empires all grew larger after 1945
The war made no difference to Asia's colonies
China became a European colony after the war
questions.explanation: By shattering the myth of Western invincibility, Japan's early victories made continued colonial rule untenable. India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon were independent by 1948 and Indonesia by 1949 — supporting the historian's judgement that decolonisation was the war's greatest consequence for Asia.
